concepts.title: Iterators and Generators
concepts.description: Every for loop runs on the iterator protocol, and generator functions use yield to pause and resume execution, producing values lazily instead of building a whole collection in memory up front.
learningObjectives: Explain the iterator protocol (__iter__, __next__, StopIteration) and what a for loop actually does under the hood.
Write a generator function using yield and explain how it pauses and resumes state between calls.
Contrast a generator function's execution model with a regular function that runs top to bottom on every call.
Explain the memory and laziness tradeoff between a generator expression and a list comprehension.
Identify a real scenario (like processing a huge file) where a generator is clearly the right choice over building a full list.

sections.heading: What a for Loop Actually Does: The Iterator Protocol
sections.body:
`for item in some_list:` is built out of two smaller pieces that any object can implement: the **iterable** protocol and the **iterator** protocol.

An **iterable** is anything with an `__iter__` method, which returns an **iterator**. An **iterator** is an object with a `__next__` method, which returns the next value each time it's called, and raises the built-in `StopIteration` exception once there's nothing left to produce. A `for` loop is syntactic sugar for calling `iter()` once (which calls `__iter__` under the hood) and then calling `next()` repeatedly (which calls `__next__`) until `StopIteration` is raised, at which point the loop ends. You never see that exception because the `for` loop catches it for you:

```python
numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# what 'for n in numbers:' does, spelled out manually:
iterator = iter(numbers)
while True:
    try:
        n = next(iterator)
    except StopIteration:
        break
    print(n)
# prints 10, 20, 30
```

This matters because it explains *why* so many different things (lists, strings, dicts, files, ranges, sets, and your own custom classes) can all be looped over with the same `for` syntax: none of them needs to be list-like, they only need to implement this two-method protocol. A list is iterable, but a list itself is *not* its own iterator: calling `iter([1,2,3])` produces a separate, fresh list-iterator object each time, which is why nested `for` loops over the same list don't interfere with each other.

sections.heading: yield: Functions That Pause and Resume
sections.body:
A regular function runs from its first line to a `return` (or the end of its body) in one uninterrupted pass each time it's called; its local state is created fresh on entry and discarded on exit. A **generator function** looks almost identical, but contains at least one `yield` statement instead of (or alongside) `return`, and that one keyword changes its execution model.

Calling a generator function does not run any of its code immediately. It returns a **generator object** (which is both an iterable and its own iterator) without executing a single line of the body yet. Each call to `next()` on that generator object runs the function's code **up to the next `yield`**, hands back the yielded value, and then **pauses execution right there**, preserving every local variable and its exact position in the code. The *next* call to `next()` resumes where it left off, rather than starting over:

```python
def count_up_to(n):
    print("starting")
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        print(f"about to yield {i}")
        yield i
        print(f"resumed after yielding {i}")
        i += 1
    print("done")

gen = count_up_to(3)   # nothing printed yet -- no code has run
print(next(gen))       # 'starting', 'about to yield 1', then returns 1
print(next(gen))       # 'resumed after yielding 1', 'about to yield 2', then returns 2
print(next(gen))       # 'resumed after yielding 2', 'about to yield 3', then returns 3
# a further next(gen) would print 'resumed after yielding 3', 'done', then raise StopIteration
```

Notice that `"starting"` doesn't print until the *first* `next()` call, not when `count_up_to(3)` itself is called: creating the generator object does no work at all. `i` keeps its value between calls, along with the line where execution paused.

sections.heading: Generator Expressions vs List Comprehensions: The Laziness Tradeoff
sections.body:
A **generator expression** looks almost identical to a list comprehension, but with parentheses instead of square brackets: `(x * 2 for x in range(1000000))` instead of `[x * 2 for x in range(1000000)]`. The two behave very differently. A list comprehension builds the **whole** list in memory immediately, all at once. A generator expression builds **nothing** up front. It creates a generator object that computes each value lazily, one at a time, only when something asks for the next one (via a `for` loop, `next()`, or being passed to something like `sum()` or `list()`).

```python
squares_list = [x * x for x in range(1_000_000)]      # allocates a full list of a million ints, right now
squares_gen = (x * x for x in range(1_000_000))         # allocates almost nothing yet

print(sum(squares_list))   # works, but the whole list existed in memory the whole time
print(sum(squares_gen))    # works too, computing and discarding one value at a time
```

Both ultimately produce the same sum, but `squares_list` requires memory proportional to a million integers, held all at once, while `squares_gen` never holds more than one value at a time in memory. This is the fundamental tradeoff: a list comprehension is the right choice when you need the whole collection available: to index into it, iterate over it multiple times, or pass it somewhere that expects a list. A generator is the right choice when you're going to consume the values once, in order, and don't need random access. You trade the ability to re-iterate or index for a dramatically smaller memory footprint, which matters enormously once the sequence is large or, as below, unbounded.

sections.heading: Processing a Huge File Line by Line
sections.body:
A common case is searching a multi-gigabyte log file for lines containing an error:

```python
def find_errors(filename):
    with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:              # a file object is itself a lazy line-by-line iterator
            if "ERROR" in line:
                yield line.rstrip("\n")

for error_line in find_errors("huge_app.log"):
    print(error_line)
```

Iterating over an open file object with `for line in f:` never loads the whole file into memory: It reads and yields one line at a time. `find_errors` is a generator function layered on top of that: it filters lazily, yielding only matching lines, one at a time, as the caller asks for them. Compare `return [line for line in f if "ERROR" in line]`. That also reads the file lazily, but it has to reach the end of the file and hold every matching line in memory before returning anything. If half of a 40 GB log matches, that's a 20 GB list. `f.read()` or `f.readlines()` would be worse: they load every line, matching or not. The generator version uses a small, constant amount of memory whatever the file size, and the caller sees the first matching line as soon as it's found.

examples.title: The for Loop, Spelled Out Manually
examples.explanation: CountdownIterator implements both halves of the protocol: __iter__ (returning itself, since it's already an iterator) and __next__ (producing the next value, or raising StopIteration once exhausted). The for loop calls iter() once, getting back the object itself, and then calls next() repeatedly (3, then 2, then 1) until __next__ raises StopIteration on the fourth call, which ends the loop. Lists, ranges, files, and dict views work the same way; writing your own class that implements __iter__ and __next__ makes it usable in a for loop, in list(), in sum(), and everywhere else Python expects an iterable. One limitation of returning self from __iter__: after one pass the object is used up, and a second loop over it produces nothing.

examples.title: A Generator Function Pausing and Resuming
examples.code:
def fibonacci_up_to(limit):
    a, b = 0, 1
    while a <= limit:
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

for num in fibonacci_up_to(20):
    print(num, end=" ")
# 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13

# Turning it into a list, if you need one:
all_values = list(fibonacci_up_to(20))
print(all_values)   # [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
examples.explanation: fibonacci_up_to is a generator function: calling it returns a generator object immediately, without computing anything. Each time the for loop asks for the next value, execution resumes right after the previous yield, with a and b holding the values they had when execution paused, computes the next Fibonacci number, and yields it, pausing again. The while loop's condition (a <= limit) is re-checked each time execution resumes, and once it's false, the generator function falls off the end, which raises StopIteration automatically, ending the for loop. list(fibonacci_up_to(20)) shows that a generator can always be converted into a full list on demand by consuming it, but doing so gives up the laziness/memory benefit, so it should only be done when you need random access or repeated iteration over all the values.

examples.title: List Comprehension vs Generator Expression: Same Values, Different Memory Behavior
examples.code:
import sys

squares_list = [x * x for x in range(100_000)]
squares_gen = (x * x for x in range(100_000))

print(sys.getsizeof(squares_list))   # about 800,000 bytes: one 8-byte pointer per element (the ints are extra)
print(sys.getsizeof(squares_gen))    # about 200 bytes, whatever the range size

print(sum(squares_list))   # 333328333350000
print(sum(squares_gen))    # 333328333350000  -- identical result, computed lazily
examples.explanation: squares_list has already materialized 100,000 integers into a list, so its size scales with the range; squares_gen is a small object that holds only the loop's current state (the underlying range iterator and the expression to apply), and its reported size would be the same even if range(100_000) were range(100_000_000) instead. Both sum() calls produce the exact same total (consuming a generator is functionally equivalent to consuming a list, one value at a time), but sum(squares_gen) never holds more than the current x*x in memory, computing, summing, and discarding each value as it goes.

misconceptions.description: A generator expression like (x*x for x in range(1000000)) still builds the whole sequence of a million values immediately -- it's basically just a list comprehension with different-looking syntax.
misconceptions.clarification: A generator expression builds nothing at all up front. It creates a lightweight generator object that computes each value lazily, one at a time, only when something requests the next one, via a for loop, next(), or being consumed by a function like sum() or list(). They trade the ability to index into the result or iterate over it more than once for a small, constant memory footprint, since only the current element needs to exist at any moment.
misconceptions.fact: A generator expression builds nothing at all up front.

misconceptions.description: Calling a generator function runs its code the same way calling a regular function does -- the difference is just that yield lets it return multiple values instead of one.
misconceptions.clarification: Calling a generator function does not execute any of its code at all. It immediately returns a generator object, with the function body still unrun. Code inside only executes when something calls next() on that generator (directly, or via a for loop), and even then, only up to the next yield statement, at which point execution pauses (preserving local variables and the exact position in the code) until the next next() call resumes it. An ordinary function can't do this: each call runs uninterrupted until it returns or raises.
misconceptions.fact: Calling a generator function does not execute any of its code at all. It immediately returns a generator object, with the function body still unrun.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and in what order?
exercises.code:
def lazy_numbers():
    print("A")
    yield 1
    print("B")
    yield 2
    print("C")

gen = lazy_numbers()
print("created generator")
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
hints: Calling lazy_numbers() itself doesn't run any code inside the function. When does the first print('A') happen?
Each next(gen) call resumes execution right where the PREVIOUS yield left off, runs until the NEXT yield (or the end), and returns whatever's yielded.
Walk through it call by call: what runs (and prints) between 'created generator' and the first next() returning, and then between the first and second next()?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'created generator', then 'A', then '1' (the returned value), then 'B', then '2'. lazy_numbers() itself runs no code; the first next(gen) runs up to the first yield (printing 'A', returning 1); the second next(gen) resumes after that yield, prints 'B', and returns 2 at the second yield.
exercises.solutionExplanation: gen = lazy_numbers() creates a generator object without executing a single line of the function body. That's why 'created generator' prints before anything from inside lazy_numbers. The first next(gen) call starts execution from the top: it prints 'A', then hits `yield 1`, which pauses execution and hands back 1, so print(next(gen)) prints '1'. The second next(gen) call resumes after that yield: it prints 'B', then hits `yield 2`, pausing again and returning 2, so print(next(gen)) prints '2'. Note that 'C' never prints in this exercise, since a third next(gen) call (which would resume after yield 2, print 'C', and then raise StopIteration on hitting the end of the function) is never made.

exercises.prompt: Write a generator function `batched(iterable, size)` that takes any iterable and a batch size, and yields successive lists (batches) of up to `size` items at a time, lazily -- it should not build the whole input into memory first. For example, list(batched(range(7), 3)) should be [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]] (the last batch may be smaller than size).
hints: You'll need to pull items from the iterable one at a time (an ordinary for loop over it works fine) and accumulate them into a temporary list until it reaches size.
Once your temporary batch list reaches `size` items, yield it, and then start a fresh, empty list for the next batch.
Don't forget the final, possibly-shorter batch: after the loop ends, if there's a partially-filled batch left over that was never yielded, yield it too.
exercises.solutionCode:
def batched(iterable, size):
    batch = []
    for item in iterable:
        batch.append(item)
        if len(batch) == size:
            yield batch
            batch = []
    if batch:              # leftover partial batch at the end
        yield batch

print(list(batched(range(7), 3)))   # [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]
print(list(batched("abcdef", 2)))   # [['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd'], ['e', 'f']]
exercises.solutionExplanation: batched accumulates items from the input iterable into a local list, batch, one at a time via an ordinary for loop. This works over any iterable (a range, a string, a list, even another generator) without requiring random access or knowing its length in advance. Once batch reaches the requested size, it's yielded (handing that batch to whoever is consuming the generator) and then reset to a fresh empty list so the next batch starts clean. Reusing the same list object after yielding it would be a bug, since the caller might still be holding a reference to the batch that was just yielded. After the for loop finishes, there may be a partial batch left over (fewer than size items, from the tail of the iterable) that was never yielded inside the loop. The final `if batch:` check yields that leftover batch too, but only if it's non-empty, which correctly handles inputs whose length is an exact multiple of size (no leftover batch to yield) as well as inputs that leave a remainder. Python 3.12 added `itertools.batched`, which does the same job but yields tuples.

assessments.prompt: What actually happens when you call a generator function, like calling gen = my_generator_function(10)?
options: No code in the function body runs yet; gen is a generator object, and code only starts executing once next() is called on it.
The function body runs immediately up to (and including) the first yield, and gen holds that first yielded value.
Python raises a TypeError, because functions containing yield cannot be called directly -- they must be used only in a for loop.
The function body runs immediately, top to bottom, and gen ends up holding whatever the last yield produced.
assessments.explanation: Calling a generator function never executes any of its body immediately: it returns a generator object right away, with execution not yet started. Code inside only begins running (up to the first yield) on the first call to next() (which a for loop performs automatically under the hood). The “The function body runs immediately, top…” and “The function body runs immediately up…” options both incorrectly assume some code runs at call time. The “Python raises a TypeError, because functions containing…” option is wrong. Calling a generator function is how you obtain the generator object; a for loop then calls next() on it for you.

assessments.prompt: You need to find and process the first line containing a specific keyword in a 40 GB log file, then stop. Which approach is most appropriate, and why?
options: Use a list comprehension, [line for line in f if keyword in line], and take the first element of the resulting list.
Load the file with f.readlines() into a list of lines, then loop over that list with a for loop.
Use `for line in f:` to iterate the open file object lazily, checking each line and breaking as soon as a match is found.
Read the whole file into one big string with f.read(), then split it into lines and search that list -- simplest to write.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the only approach that never requires the full 40 GB file to exist in memory at once. Iterating an open file object with a for loop reads and yields one line at a time, lazily, and break stops iteration (and further reading) the moment a match is found, without touching the rest of the file at all. The “Read the whole file into one big…” and “Load the file with f.readlines() into…” options load all 40 GB into memory before any searching happens. The “Use a list comprehension, [line for line…” option stores only the matching lines, but it can't stop early: it reads to the end of the file even if the match is on line one.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who understands regular functions but has never seen yield before, what makes a generator function fundamentally different from a regular function -- not just in syntax, but in execution model.
assessments.modelAnswer: A regular function, once called, runs from its first line to a return statement or the end of its body in one uninterrupted pass. Every call starts fresh, and once the function returns, all of its local state is gone. A generator function, any function containing at least one yield statement, behaves completely differently. Calling it doesn't run any of its code at all; it immediately hands back a generator object, an iterator that remembers where execution should begin. Only when something calls next() on that generator object does any code run, and even then, only up to the next yield statement: at that point execution pauses, mid-function, with every local variable's current value and the exact line of code preserved, not discarded the way a regular function's locals are on return. The next call to next() doesn't restart the function from the top; it resumes execution from that paused point, continuing until it hits another yield (pausing again) or reaches the end of the function body (which raises StopIteration automatically, signaling there's nothing left). So a generator is more than 'a function that can return multiple things': it keeps suspended execution state between calls, and that lets it produce values one at a time, only when asked for, instead of computing everything up front.

assessments.prompt:
```python
nums = [1, 2, 3]
it1 = iter(nums)
it2 = iter(nums)

print(next(it1))
print(next(it1))
print(next(it2))
```
What gets printed, in order?
options: It raises StopIteration on the third call, since nums has already been exhausted by it1
assessments.explanation: `iter(nums)` returns a brand-new, independent iterator object each time it's called: `it1` and `it2` are two separate iterators over the same underlying list, each tracking its own position. Advancing `it1` twice (getting `1`, then `2`) has no effect on `it2`, which starts from the beginning of `nums` and hasn't been advanced at all yet, so its first `next()` call returns `1`. Two for loops over the same list stay independent for the same reason: each makes its own call to `iter()`.

assessments.prompt:
```python
gen = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
print(list(gen))
print(list(gen))
```
What gets printed?
options: RuntimeError: generator already executing
assessments.explanation: The first `list(gen)` fully consumes the generator, pulling every value until it's exhausted, producing `[0, 2, 4]`. A generator has no way to 'rewind' or reset itself. Once it's exhausted (its underlying code has run to completion and raised `StopIteration`), every subsequent attempt to pull a value from it, including a second `list(gen)`, hits that same exhausted state and produces nothing: an empty list. A list can be iterated over as many times as you like, but a generator can only be consumed once, in one pass.

concepts.title: Context Managers
concepts.description: The with statement guarantees cleanup code runs even when an exception occurs, by relying on an object's __enter__/__exit__ methods (the same guarantee try/finally provides, in reusable form).
learningObjectives: Explain what the with statement does and how it relates to __enter__ and __exit__.
Explain why with guarantees cleanup even when an exception is raised inside its block.
Connect the with statement's guarantee to try/finally, and explain why with is usually the cleaner choice.
Write a simple custom context manager using contextlib.contextmanager and a generator function.
Identify common real-world use cases for context managers beyond files, such as locks.

sections.heading: The with Statement and the __enter__ / __exit__ Protocol
sections.body:
The `with` statement wraps a block of code with guaranteed setup and teardown logic, delegated to an object that implements the **context manager protocol**: an `__enter__` method (called when the `with` block starts) and an `__exit__` method (called when the block ends, for any reason at all, including an exception).

```python
class Announcer:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("Entering the block")
        return self   # this becomes the value bound by 'as', if used

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print("Exiting the block")
        return False   # False means: don't suppress any exception that occurred

with Announcer() as a:
    print("Inside the block")

# Entering the block
# Inside the block
# Exiting the block
```

`with Announcer() as a:` calls `Announcer().__enter__()` and binds whatever it returns to `a`; when the indented block finishes, normally or via an exception, Python calls `__exit__` automatically. `__exit__` receives three arguments describing any exception that occurred (`exc_type`, `exc_value`, `traceback`, all `None` if the block finished normally), and its return value decides whether that exception should be suppressed (`True`) or allowed to keep propagating (`False`, or nothing, since `None` is falsy). Most context managers return `False`/`None`, so they clean up without swallowing errors.

sections.heading: Why This Matters: Cleanup Even When Things Go Wrong
sections.body:
`with` guarantees that `__exit__` runs **no matter how the block ends**, whether it finishes normally, hits a `return`/`break`/`continue` that jumps out early, or raises an exception that propagates all the way through. Resource cleanup depends on this: closing a file, releasing a lock, closing a database connection, or committing/rolling back a transaction. Without the guarantee, an exception raised partway through a block could skip right past cleanup code that comes after it:

```python
f = open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8")
data = f.read()
process(data)   # if this raises an exception...
f.close()       # ...this line is never reached -- file stays open
```

If `process(data)` raises, the exception propagates immediately, skipping every line after it in this straight-line code, including `f.close()`. This is the same problem `try/finally` was designed to solve, and `with` is built on top of that same guarantee: `__exit__` runs the way a `finally` block runs, regardless of whether the `try` body succeeded or raised. In fact, `with obj:` is roughly equivalent to the code below (the one thing it leaves out is that a true return value from `__exit__` suppresses the exception):

```python
# pseudocode for 'with obj as x: BODY' (needs 'import sys'):
x = obj.__enter__()
try:
    BODY
finally:
    obj.__exit__(*sys.exc_info())
```

`with` packages the setup and the guaranteed teardown into one reusable object, so each caller doesn't have to write the `try/finally` again and get it right.

sections.heading: contextlib.contextmanager: A Lighter Way to Write One
sections.body:
Writing a full class with `__enter__` and `__exit__` is sometimes more ceremony than a simple context manager needs. The `contextlib.contextmanager` decorator lets you write one using an ordinary generator function instead. The code before the single `yield` becomes `__enter__`'s logic, the yielded value becomes what `as` binds, and the code after the `yield` (typically inside a `try/finally` of its own) becomes `__exit__`'s logic:

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def announced_block():
    print("Entering the block")
    try:
        yield "some value"   # execution pauses here for the whole 'with' body
    finally:
        print("Exiting the block")

with announced_block() as value:
    print(f"Inside the block, got: {value}")

# Entering the block
# Inside the block, got: some value
# Exiting the block
```

This relies on the generator pause/resume mechanics from the Iterators and Generators concept: the `with` block calls `next()` on the generator once to run everything up to `yield`, treating that as `__enter__`; the `with` block's body then runs; and when the block ends, the `with` machinery resumes the generator (with `next()` if the block finished normally, or `.throw()` if an exception occurred), running everything after `yield`, treating that as `__exit__`. Wrapping the post-yield code in `try/finally` (as shown above) is important so that cleanup still runs even if the `with` block itself raises. The exception gets thrown back into the generator at the point of the `yield`, and `finally` ensures the cleanup code after it still executes before that exception propagates onward.

sections.heading: Common Use Cases: Files, Locks, and Beyond
sections.body:
The context manager you'll use most is `open()` for files. `with open("data.txt") as f:` guarantees `f.close()` runs even if reading or processing the file raises an exception midway through (the File Handling concept goes into detail). Another everyday use case is **locks**, used for coordinating access to shared resources across threads:

```python
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()

def update_shared_counter():
    with lock:              # acquires the lock on entry
        # ... critical section: only one thread executes this at a time ...
        pass
    # lock is released automatically here, even if the critical section raised
```

`with lock:` calls `lock.acquire()` on entry and guarantees `lock.release()` on exit. That matters because a lock that's acquired but never released due to an unexpected exception would deadlock every other thread waiting on it forever. Any pair of actions where the second must follow the first (open/close, acquire/release, connect/disconnect, start/stop a timer) is a candidate for a context manager.

examples.title: Custom Context Manager as a Class
examples.code:
import time

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        print(f"Elapsed: {elapsed:.4f} seconds")
        return False   # don't suppress exceptions

with Timer():
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))

print(total)
examples.explanation: __enter__ records the start time and returns self (unused here, since the with statement has no `as` clause, but available if needed). __exit__ computes and prints the elapsed time regardless of what happened inside the block. If `sum(range(1_000_000))` had raised an exception instead of completing normally, __exit__ would still run and print the elapsed time before that exception continued propagating, because __exit__ is guaranteed to run on the way out of a with block, exception or not. Returning False from __exit__ means any exception that did occur is not swallowed; it keeps propagating normally after cleanup runs.

examples.title: The Same Timer, Written with contextlib.contextmanager
examples.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timer():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print(f"Elapsed: {elapsed:.4f} seconds")

with timer():
    total = sum(range(1_000_000))

print(total)
examples.explanation: This produces identical behavior to the class-based Timer, with noticeably less code. The lines before yield run as __enter__ would; yield (with nothing after it, since there's no `as` clause used here) pauses the generator for the duration of the with block's body; and the finally block, which runs when the generator is resumed as the with block ends, plays the role of __exit__. And because it's wrapped in try/finally, it still runs and prints the elapsed time even if the with block's body raises an exception, since the generator gets that exception thrown back in at the yield point, and finally guarantees the cleanup code after it still executes.

examples.title: with vs a Hand-Written try/finally
examples.code:
def risky_operation():
    raise ValueError("something went wrong")

# Manual try/finally version
lock_held = True
try:
    print("lock acquired (simulated)")
    risky_operation()
finally:
    lock_held = False
    print("lock released (simulated)")

# print("unreachable") -- the ValueError still propagates past this point after finally runs
examples.explanation: Even though risky_operation() raises a ValueError, the finally block still runs: 'lock released (simulated)' prints, before the exception continues propagating up and (in this snippet, since it's never caught) crashes the program. A with statement provides the same guarantee via __exit__. A lock object's __enter__/__exit__ methods do this acquire/release pairing internally, which is why `with lock:` is preferred over manually calling lock.acquire() and lock.release(). You can't forget the release() call, or put it somewhere an exception could skip past.

misconceptions.description: with is just a shorter way to write code -- it doesn't provide any guarantee that plain sequential code couldn't also provide if you're careful.
misconceptions.clarification: with adds a guarantee as well as brevity: __exit__ is called however the block ends, whether normally, via an early return/break/continue, or because an exception propagated through it. Plain sequential code has no such guarantee. A line like f.close() written after some risky operation is skipped if that operation raises, since the exception propagates immediately past every subsequent line. Getting the same guarantee without with requires a try/finally, which with packages up in an object's __enter__/__exit__ methods, so callers get it without writing their own.
misconceptions.fact: with adds a guarantee as well as brevity: __exit__ is called however the block ends, whether normally, via an early return/break/continue, or because an exception propagated through it.

misconceptions.description: A context manager's __exit__ method, if it returns something, always suppresses any exception that occurred inside the with block.
misconceptions.clarification: __exit__'s return value controls this: returning a truthy value (normally True) tells Python to suppress the exception. The with statement exits normally as if nothing happened, and the exception does not propagate further. Returning a falsy value (False, or not returning anything, which defaults to None) means the exception, if there was one, continues propagating after __exit__ finishes its cleanup. The vast majority of context managers should return False/None, since swallowing exceptions is rarely correct behavior. An __exit__ that returns True by accident makes errors vanish without a trace.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, including whether the exception message appears?
hints: __exit__ is guaranteed to run when the with block ends for ANY reason, including an exception being raised inside it. Track when that happens relative to the raise.
__exit__ returns False here. What does that tell Python to do with the ValueError after __exit__ finishes running?
Order the four possible outputs: 'enter', 'inside', 'exit', and 'caught: boom'. Figure out which happens before which.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'enter', then 'inside', then 'exit', then 'caught: boom'. __exit__ runs (printing 'exit') before the ValueError propagates out of the with block; since __exit__ returns False, the exception isn't suppressed, so it continues propagating and gets caught by the outer try/except, printing 'caught: boom' last.
exercises.solutionExplanation: with Guard(): calls __enter__ first, printing 'enter'. The block's body then prints 'inside' and raises ValueError('boom'). Because with guarantees __exit__ runs regardless of how the block ends, __exit__ runs next, printing 'exit', receiving the exception's details as its arguments. __exit__ returns False, which tells Python not to suppress the exception. So after __exit__ finishes, the ValueError continues propagating as if the with statement weren't there, and it's caught by the surrounding try/except ValueError, printing 'caught: boom'. If __exit__ had returned True instead, the exception would have been suppressed, and 'caught: boom' would never print.

exercises.prompt: Using contextlib.contextmanager, write a context manager function `suppressing(*exception_types)` that suppresses (ignores) any exception of the given type(s) raised inside its with block, letting the program continue normally after the with statement -- similar in spirit to contextlib's own suppress(). For example, `with suppressing(ZeroDivisionError): 1 / 0` should not raise.
hints: You'll need a try/except (not just try/finally) around the yield, since you're not just cleaning up. You're catching and discarding a specific exception.
Catch the exception with `except exception_types as e:`. Since exception_types is a tuple of types (from *args), except can accept a tuple.
Catching the exception and doing nothing else in that except block (or a bare `pass`) is enough to suppress it. You don't need to re-raise it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: suppressing wraps the with block's body (represented by yield) in a try/except targeting the exception types passed in as exception_types (a tuple, thanks to *args). If the with block raises one of those types, the generator's except clause catches it right at the yield point (since a with block's exception gets thrown back into the generator there), and doing nothing in the except body (pass) means the exception is discarded. It never propagates further, so execution continues normally right after the with statement. Note this does NOT use try/finally the way the earlier timer example did: finally would let cleanup code run but would still allow the exception to keep propagating afterward, whereas try/except followed by no re-raise is what suppresses it. An exception type not listed in exception_types would not match the except clause and would propagate normally, as intended.

assessments.prompt: What is the with statement's core guarantee, compared to writing the equivalent setup/teardown logic as plain sequential code?
options: with guarantees the context manager's __exit__ method runs when the block ends, whether it completes normally, exits early, or raises an exception -- the same guarantee try/finally provides.
with only guarantees cleanup runs if the block completes without raising any exception.
with is purely a stylistic convenience with no behavioral guarantee beyond what plain sequential code already provides.
with guarantees that any exception raised inside the block will always be suppressed automatically.
assessments.explanation: The defining feature of with is that __exit__ is guaranteed to run no matter how the block ends, including when an exception propagates through it, which is the guarantee a try/finally block provides, just packaged into a reusable object's protocol instead of requiring hand-written try/finally at every call site. The “with only guarantees cleanup runs…” option has the guarantee backwards (it also covers the exception case, not just the success case). The “with is purely a stylistic convenience…” option understates it. Plain sequential code has no such guarantee, since an exception skips all subsequent lines. The “with guarantees that any exception raised inside…” option is wrong. Whether an exception is suppressed depends on __exit__'s return value, and most context managers do not suppress exceptions.

assessments.prompt: Explain how contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator function into a context manager, and why the code after yield is typically wrapped in a try/finally.
assessments.modelAnswer: contextlib.contextmanager lets you define a context manager using a generator function that yields once, instead of writing a full class with separate __enter__ and __exit__ methods. When the resulting object is used in a with statement, entering the block resumes the generator up to its yield. This is effectively __enter__'s job, and whatever value is yielded becomes what an `as` clause binds. The with block's body then executes. When that body finishes (or raises), the with machinery resumes the generator again, either normally (if the block completed without an exception) or by throwing the exception back into the generator at the exact point of the yield (if the block raised one). And whatever code comes after yield plays the role of __exit__. Wrapping that post-yield code in try/finally matters because of the exception case: if the with block's body raises, that exception is thrown into the generator right at the yield, and without a try/finally around it, the cleanup code after yield would never run, since the thrown exception would propagate straight out of the generator before reaching it. Putting the cleanup in a finally block guarantees it still executes (printing a log message, releasing a resource, closing a connection) before that exception is allowed to continue propagating out of the with statement, which matches what a hand-written __exit__ method does.

assessments.prompt:
```python
class Silencer:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print("exit ran")
        return True

with Silencer():
    print("before")
    raise ValueError("oops")
print("after the with block")
```
What gets printed?
options: before / exit ran (but the program crashes anyway, since __exit__ can only suppress built-in exceptions, not user-raised ones)
before / exit ran, and then the ValueError still propagates and crashes the program
exit ran / before / after the with block
before / exit ran / after the with block
assessments.explanation: "before" prints, then `raise ValueError("oops")` fires. `__exit__` still runs, as guaranteed, printing "exit ran" and receiving the exception's details as its three arguments. Because `__exit__` returns `True`, a truthy value, Python suppresses the exception: it does not continue propagating after `__exit__` finishes. Execution then continues normally right after the `with` statement, printing "after the with block". `__exit__` treats every exception type identically for this purpose. There's no distinction between built-in and user-defined exceptions in how the return value is interpreted.

assessments.prompt:
```python
class Inspector:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print(exc_type, exc_value)
        return False

with Inspector():
    print("no problems here")
```
What gets printed?
options: no problems here / <class 'NoneType'> <class 'NoneType'>
no problems here / None None
no problems here -- __exit__ is never actually called at all, since no exception occurred
None None / no problems here
assessments.explanation: `__exit__` runs unconditionally when the `with` block ends, whether or not an exception occurred. That's the whole point of the guarantee. Since the block here completes normally with no exception raised, Python calls `__exit__(None, None, None)`: all three of `exc_type`, `exc_value`, and `traceback` are the value `None` (not the class `NoneType`), documenting 'nothing went wrong.' So after "no problems here" prints from inside the block, `__exit__` runs and prints `None None`.

assessments.prompt:
```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def broken_context():
    print("setup")
    yield
    print("teardown")   # NOT wrapped in try/finally

with broken_context():
    print("body")
    raise ValueError("bad")
```
What happens?
options: The program hangs, because a generator with no try/finally around yield cannot be resumed after an exception
setup / teardown / body, with no error at all
setup / body print, then the ValueError propagates uncaught -- "teardown" never prints
setup / body / teardown, and then the ValueError propagates
assessments.explanation: "setup" prints, then `yield` pauses the generator for the with block's body. "body" prints, then the `raise ValueError("bad")` fires. And because the block raised, the `with` machinery resumes the generator by throwing that exception back in at the exact point of `yield`. With no `try/finally` (or `try/except`) wrapped around the `yield`, the generator has nothing to catch it with, so the exception propagates straight out of the generator function immediately. `print("teardown")`, sitting after the unprotected `yield`, is never reached. Wrapping the `yield` in `try/finally` fixes it.

concepts.title: Type Hints
concepts.description: Type hints document expected argument and return types for humans, IDEs, and static checkers like mypy, but Python itself never enforces them at runtime, which surprises many developers coming from statically-typed languages.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of type hints: documentation, IDE support, and enabling static checkers like mypy.
State precisely why type hints are not enforced at runtime, and predict what happens when code violates its own hints.
Write basic type hints for variables and function signatures.
Use Optional/Union (or the X | None syntax) to express a value that may be one of several types or may be absent.
Explain gradual typing and why a codebase can mix hinted and unhinted code.

sections.heading: Why Type Hints Exist
Type Hints Are Not Enforced at Runtime
sections.body:
Developers coming from Java, C#, or Go often assume otherwise, so to be clear: **the interpreter does not check type hints at runtime.** It stores them and moves on. Code that violates its own type hints runs without complaint:

```python
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add("hello", "world"))   # 'helloworld' -- runs fine! No TypeError, no warning.
print(add(2, 3))                # 5
```

`add("hello", "world")` violates the hint `a: int, b: int`, and Python runs it anyway, because `+` happens to also work on strings, concatenating them. The hints exist as **metadata**, stored on the function object (inspectable via `add.__annotations__`) for tools to read. Some libraries choose to read them (dataclasses to find fields, Pydantic to validate input), but a plain function call never does. Catching this kind of mistake requires *running* a separate static type checker like `mypy` as a step in your workflow (locally, or in CI). It will not happen automatically just because you wrote the hints. Writing accurate hints and then never running a checker against them gives you the *appearance* of type safety and nothing more.

sections.heading: Basic Syntax for Variables and Functions
sections.body:
Variable annotations use a colon: `age: int = 30`, or even without an initial value, `age: int` (which just records the intended type without creating the variable at all. Referencing `age` before assigning it would still raise `NameError`, as it would with no annotation). Function signatures annotate each parameter the same way, and the return type is written after `->`:

```python
name: str = "Amy"
scores: list = [85, 90, 78]         # a bare 'list' says 'a list of something', unspecified
tagged_scores: list[int] = [85, 90, 78]   # more precise: a list of ints

def average(numbers: list[int]) -> float:
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
```

`list[int]` (using square brackets on the built-in `list`, valid since Python 3.9) is more informative than a bare `list`, since it also documents what the list is expected to contain. Before 3.9, the equivalent was `List[int]` with `from typing import List`. You'll still see that style in older codebases.

sections.heading: Optional and Union: Expressing 'Could Be One of Several Types'
sections.body:
Many values can legitimately be one of several types, most commonly 'this type, or `None`.' `Optional[X]` (from the `typing` module) means `Union[X, None]`, 'an `X`, or `None`.' `Union[X, Y]` more generally means 'an `X` or a `Y`.' Modern Python (3.10+) supports a shorter built-in syntax using `|`, which most new code now prefers:

```python
from typing import Optional, Union

def find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[str]:      # returns a str, or None if not found
    ...

def find_user_modern(user_id: int) -> str | None:    # equivalent, Python 3.10+ syntax
    ...

def parse_id(raw: Union[str, int]) -> int:           # accepts either a str or an int
    return int(raw)

def parse_id_modern(raw: str | int) -> int:          # equivalent, Python 3.10+ syntax
    return int(raw)
```

A function hinted to return `Optional[str]` (or `str | None`) is documenting, and letting a type checker verify, that callers must handle the `None` case; mypy flags `find_user(5).upper()` when there's no `None` check first. Python itself would only raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` at runtime, and only on the calls where the function returns `None`.

sections.heading: Gradual Typing: You Don't Have to Hint Everything
sections.body:
Python's type hint system is designed around **gradual typing**: you can add hints to some functions and variables while leaving others completely unhinted, and mix both freely within the same file, module, or codebase. Checkers treat an unhinted parameter as `Any`, a type that's compatible with everything, and mypy by default doesn't even check the body of a function with no hints at all. Unhinted local variables inside a checked function are different: their types are inferred from what you assign to them.

So you can add hints to a large existing codebase function by function; quick scripts and prototypes can skip hints without any tooling complaint, and add them later if the code graduates into something more permanent; and third-party libraries without their own hints (or with incomplete ones) don't block you from hinting *your own* code that uses them, since the boundary just falls back to `Any` there. The cost is that coverage is easy to overestimate. Once a codebase is mostly hinted, teams usually turn on mypy's `--disallow-untyped-defs` (part of `--strict`) so that an unhinted function becomes an error rather than a hole in the checking.

examples.title: Hints Are Metadata, Not Enforcement
examples.explanation: divide("10", "2") does raise an error, but that TypeError comes from the / operator not supporting two strings, not from Python checking the a: int hint and rejecting the call for violating it; divide(10.5, 2) makes it clearer: it violates the a: int hint (10.5 is a float, not an int) and runs without a warning, producing 5.25, because float division works whatever the hint says. __annotations__ shows that the hints are stored as a dict on the function object, available for tools to inspect, but never consulted by the interpreter when the function is called.

examples.title: Optional and the None-Handling It Documents
examples.explanation: The -> Optional[int] hint documents, for both human readers and a static checker, that this function might return an int OR might return None. Callers are expected to handle both cases. The if result is not None: check does that. The commented-out final line shows what happens if a caller ignores the hint's implication and doesn't check for None: Python raises a TypeError at the point of using result2 as if it were guaranteed to be an int, but only when that code path runs (here, only when the list has no negative numbers). A static checker like mypy would flag `result2 + 1` as an error immediately, without needing to run the code or hit that specific input at all.

examples.title: Gradual Typing: Mixing Hinted and Unhinted Code
examples.explanation: hinted_total has full type hints; unhinted_discount has none at all. Both run identically well. Python doesn't care either way, since it never enforces hints regardless of whether they're present. A static checker treats unhinted_discount's parameters as the implicit Any type, so it won't flag anything about how they're used. Because its return type is Any too, final_price is unchecked as well: the gap spreads to whatever consumes the result. This mixture is normal in Python codebases: hints get added where they're most valuable (public APIs, complex logic, anything a team wants a type checker to help enforce) and the rest can wait.

misconceptions.description: If a function has a type hint like def f(x: int), calling it with a string, like f("hello"), will raise a TypeError because Python enforces the hint.
misconceptions.clarification: Python's runtime does not check type hints at all. Calling f("hello") runs the function body as written, using whatever value was passed, regardless of what the hint says. If an error occurs, it's because some operation inside the function's body fails for that type (e.g. x + 1 when x is a string), not because Python compared the argument against the hint and rejected the call. Catching a hint violation before runtime requires running a separate static type checker like mypy as a, step. It is not something that happens automatically just because hints are present in the code.

misconceptions.description: Once you start using type hints in a project, you have to hint every function, parameter, and variable, or the type checker (and Python itself) will complain.
misconceptions.clarification: Python's type hint system is designed for gradual typing: hinted and unhinted code can coexist freely, in the same function, file, or codebase, with no requirement to hint everything. Python itself never complains about missing hints. A static checker like mypy, at its default settings, treats any unhinted parameter as the implicit Any type, which is compatible with everything and produces no type-checking errors. It means that particular piece of code is not being type-checked, not that it's wrong. This lets teams add hints incrementally, function by function, rather than needing to hint a codebase before gaining any benefit at all.
misconceptions.fact: Python's type hint system is designed for gradual typing: hinted and unhinted code can coexist freely, in the same function, file, or codebase, with no requirement to hint everything.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? Does it raise any error?
exercises.code:
def label(value: int) -> str:
    return f"Value: {value}"

print(label(42))
print(label(3.14))
print(label("already a string"))
hints: Only one of these three calls passes an int. Does Python check the hint `value: int` before running the function body?
f-strings can format basically any value into a string representation. Would an f"{value}" ever fail just because value isn't an int?
Trace what f"Value: {value}" produces for each of the three different types of argument passed in.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'Value: 42', 'Value: 3.14', 'Value: already a string'. All three print successfully with no error at all. The int hint is never checked or enforced by Python; f-strings can format any value regardless of its type.
exercises.solutionExplanation: value: int is purely a hint. Python's runtime never checks it before or during the call, so label(3.14) and label("already a string") run like label(42) does, just substituting whatever value was passed into the f-string. f"Value: {value}" works for essentially any object (it calls str() on whatever value holds internally), so there's no operation inside the function body that would fail for a float or a string either. All three calls succeed and print, with no errors or warnings: the int hint has no runtime effect. A separate checker would catch it (mypy would report label(3.14) and label("already a string") as type errors, without ever running this code).

exercises.prompt: Write a function `safe_divide(a: float, b: float) -> Optional[float]` that returns the result of a / b, or None if b is zero (avoiding a ZeroDivisionError). Include the type hints exactly as specified, remembering that a return type of Optional[float] means the function can return either a float or None.
hints: You'll need `from typing import Optional` to use Optional in the hint.
Check whether b == 0 before dividing, and return None in that specific case instead of performing the division.
The Optional[float] return hint is just documentation for callers and tools. It doesn't change how you write the function's logic, just what you choose to return in each branch.
exercises.solutionExplanation: safe_divide checks b == 0 first and returns None in that case, avoiding the ZeroDivisionError that a / b would otherwise raise. In every other case, it returns the ordinary float result of the division. The Optional[float] return hint documents both possible outcomes for anyone reading the signature or using a static checker. It signals that callers should be prepared to receive None and should check for it (with `is not None`, as in the usage example) before treating the result as a float. Python does nothing with the hint at runtime.

assessments.prompt:
```python
def combine(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

result = combine([1, 2], [3, 4])
print(result)
```
What happens when this runs?
options: Python raises a TypeError immediately when combine is called, because [1, 2] and [3, 4] don't match the int hints.
It prints [1, 2, 3, 4], since + concatenates lists, and Python never checks the a: int / b: int hints at runtime.
It raises a TypeError, but only because mypy is silently run automatically whenever a type-hinted function is called.
It raises a SyntaxError, because type hints require their declared types to be enforced at the point of definition.
assessments.explanation: Python's runtime never checks type hints, so calling combine([1, 2], [3, 4]) runs the function body as written, with a and b bound to the list arguments passed in. Inside, a + b uses list concatenation (since + is defined for lists), producing [1, 2, 3, 4]. No error occurs at all, despite blatantly violating the a: int, b: int hints. The “Python raises a TypeError immediately when combine…” and “It raises a TypeError, but only…” options both incorrectly assume some runtime or automatic type-checking occurs. Catching this would require running a separate tool like mypy as a step, which never happens implicitly. The “It raises a SyntaxError, because type hints…” option is wrong. Annotations are valid syntax whatever values you later pass.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer says: 'I added type hints to all my function signatures, so now my code is type-safe.' Explain what's true and what's missing from that statement.
assessments.modelAnswer: It's true that adding type hints is worthwhile. Hints document intended types in the code, improve IDE autocomplete and inline help, and make it possible for a separate static type checker like mypy, pyright, or pyre to analyze the codebase and catch type-related mistakes without ever running it. What's missing is the word 'now': writing the hints themselves does not make the code type-safe by itself, because Python's interpreter does nothing with type hints at runtime. It doesn't check them, validate them, or enforce them in any way. A function hinted as def add(a: int, b: int) -> int can be called with completely mismatched types, like strings or lists, and Python will run it without complaint, doing whatever the function's code happens to do with those values (which might work by accident, might raise a totally unrelated error, or might produce a wrong result). The hints only become a safety net once a static type checker is run against the code (as a manual step locally, or (much more reliably) wired into CI so it runs on every change), and its output is acted on. So what's missing is the checker: the safety comes from accurate hints plus a checker whose findings get fixed.

assessments.prompt:
```python
def transform(value: str, factor: int = 2) -> list:
    return [value] * factor

print(transform.__annotations__)
```
What gets printed?
options: {} -- since transform has never actually been called, its annotations haven't been generated yet
{'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': <class 'int'>} -- with no 'return' key, since return hints aren't stored in __annotations__
{'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': 2, 'return': <class 'list'>}
{'value': <class 'str'>, 'factor': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'list'>}
assessments.explanation: Type hints are stored as plain metadata on the function object the moment it's defined. Calling the function isn't required for `__annotations__` to exist. The dict maps each hinted parameter name to its annotated type object, and includes a `'return'` key for the `-> list` annotation. Note that the default value `2` for `factor` does not appear in `__annotations__` at all. Only the *type hint* `int` does; defaults are a separate mechanism (visible instead via `__defaults__`) that `__annotations__` has nothing to do with.

assessments.prompt: Which pair of type hints are exactly equivalent in meaning?
options: Optional[str] and Union[str, None]
Union[str, None] and plain str, since None is just treated as a valid str value
Optional[str] and str | int
Optional[str] and Union[str, int]
assessments.explanation: `Optional[X]` is defined to mean `Union[X, None]`, 'an X, or None', so `Optional[str]` and `Union[str, None]` are the identical hint written two different ways. `Union[str, int]` (“Optional[str] and Union[str, int]”) means 'a str or an int,' with no mention of None at all. Not equivalent. The “Union[str, None] and plain str, since None…” option is wrong on two counts: `None` is not a valid `str` value, and dropping it from the hint changes the meaning. The “Optional[str] and str | int” option pairs `Optional[str]` (str-or-None) against `str | int` (str-or-int), which describes a completely different set of allowed types.

assessments.prompt: A codebase has a function `def calculate(a, b): return a + b` with no type hints at all, sitting alongside several fully type-hinted functions elsewhere in the same file. Which statement is accurate?
options: calculate() runs measurably slower than a hinted equivalent, since Python must infer its parameter types at every call
mypy refuses to check any of the hinted functions in the file until every function in that file has hints
Python runs calculate() exactly the same way it would run any hinted function -- hints are never enforced either way
Python raises a SyntaxError, because hinted and unhinted functions cannot coexist in the same file
assessments.explanation: Python's gradual typing model means hinted and unhinted code freely coexist, in the same function, file, or codebase, with zero restriction. Python itself never enforces hints on any function regardless of whether they're present, so calculate() runs identically to a hinted version. A static checker like mypy treats an unhinted parameter as the implicit `Any` type (compatible with everything, and not an error), which lets teams add hints incrementally without needing an all-or-nothing rewrite before gaining any benefit. Calls run at the same speed either way.
